title: KPI Copilot Profile v1.0
description: Settings that map a team workflow onto the shared KPI engine. Start small; account and project overrides hold only what differs. Generated workbooks expose settings and evidence for review.

x-workbook.label: Role
x-workbook.hint: e.g. Software Project Lead

x-workbook.label: Client account / business unit
x-workbook.hint: e.g. Northwind. Used to name output folders.

x-workbook.label: Timezone
x-workbook.hint: Dates in notes are written in this timezone.

x-workbook.title: Things that are the same for everyone in the company
x-workbook.readonly_hint: Do not change these unless the company changes. They are what makes one lead's KPIs comparable with another's.

kpi_registry.description: Local cache of the KPI definitions read from PMS: ids, names, the official descriptions, the default targets, and the targets each project sets for itself. Refreshed by scripts/kpi_registry.py --refresh. Never hand-edited - a target changed in PMS is picked up by the next refresh, and a target changed here would make the workbook and PMS disagree.

x-workbook.label: KPI definition cache
x-workbook.hint: Synced from PMS. Read-only.

note_format.default: what the numbers say, in sentences || what was left out || why

x-workbook.label: Note format
x-workbook.hint: Fixed company-wide so management reads every project the same way.

x-workbook.label: Require evidence on every judgement
x-workbook.hint: Yes = a Yes/No with no link is flagged in review.

note_style.description: How the generated part of a KPI note is worded. sentences (default): whole sentences, the way a person would write them. fragments: the older 'heading || numbers || what was left out'. It changes the wording only, never a figure.

tools.description: The tool registry: every place your projects' truth lives, with a plain-language note on what it is for. One registry covers all your projects - list the Google Chat space for one account and the Slack channel for another, and tag each with the projects it belongs to. A tool with no projects listed is available to all of them (PMS, your Drive folder). This is what lets Claude find things without being told each time, and what lets a new team member understand the setup at a glance.

id.description: Short handle used elsewhere in the profile, e.g. 'tracker', 'chat-devqa', 'plan-doc'.

kind.description: What sort of thing it is. Drives which steps can use it.

name.description: What people call it, e.g. 'Asana', 'Northwind Dev-QA'.

url_or_id.description: Link, space id, sheet id or folder id.

description.description: One sentence: what this is and why it matters. Written for a person who has never seen the project.

used_for.description: Which parts of a KPI run read or write this.

access.description: How to get in, e.g. 'Google SSO', 'Atlassian account'. Never a credential.

projects.description: Project ids this tool belongs to. Leave empty when it applies to all of them, such as PMS or a shared Drive folder.

accounts.description: Account ids this tool belongs to. A Google Chat space for one client and a Slack channel for another live side by side here, each tagged with its account.

people.description: Who is in this space or owns this document, as their names appear in it. Optional, but it is how somebody new to the account finds out who to ask, and it is what lets a run tell a client-reported defect from a QA-reported one when the tracker does not say.

client_facing.description: Is the client in here. A client-facing space is where agreed dates get set and where a client-found defect first appears; an internal one is not. Marking it wrong is how a date somebody agreed in a client call gets treated as an internal decision.

note.description: Anything else worth knowing: quirks, when it is quiet, what NOT to trust in it.

adapter.description: Which reader turns your tracker into a board. Ships with: asana, jira (Cloud, Server, Data Center), github (Issues, and a Projects board's status), and csv - which works with an export from any tracker at all. A reader for another tracker is one small file; see adapters/_contract.md.

x-workbook.label: Adapter
x-workbook.hint: asana | jira | csv (csv = export from anything)

x-workbook.label: Board / project reference
x-workbook.hint: Asana: the number after /project/. Jira: the project key, e.g. SAV.

x-workbook.label: Field holding story points
x-workbook.hint: Leave blank if you measure in hours.

x-workbook.label: Field holding the ticket key
x-workbook.hint: Leave blank to use the tracker's own id.

options.description: Reader-specific extras. asana: include_subtasks, token_env. jira: jql (read this query instead of the whole project). github: project (a Projects board such as orgs/acme/projects/7, whose Status field becomes the status), status_field, graphql_url (GitHub Enterprise Server), max_items. Also defect_field / defect_board when conventions.defect_by needs them.

conventions.description: How your team names and shapes things. These are regular expressions or literal lists - the setup interview proposes them by looking at your board, and you correct what it got wrong.

additional_request_label.description: Client wording for approved added work in notes, for example Additional Request. Internal types and PMS identifiers do not change.

grouping.description: Count member tickets of approved source groups individually while retaining the group's estimate once.

x-workbook.label: Ticket key looks like
x-workbook.hint: Regex, e.g. TKT-\d+ or [A-Z]+-\d+. Blank = use the tracker id.

x-workbook.label: A defect is recognised by
x-workbook.hint: Regex on the title, e.g. ^(Bug|Observation|Improvement) ?\d+ - or leave blank and use defect_by below.

x-workbook.label: How defects are marked
x-workbook.hint: title-pattern | issue-type | label | separate-board | field

x-workbook.label: Values that mean 'defect'
x-workbook.hint: e.g. Bug, Defect - used when marked by issue type, label or field.

x-workbook.label: Values that mean 'observation / improvement'
x-workbook.hint: Reported, but not counted as defects by default.

exclude_patterns.description: Cards that are not deliverables: QA admin cards, milestone markers, grouping/umbrella cards, duplicates.

x-workbook.label: Not a deliverable when the title matches
x-workbook.hint: One regex per line.

assignee_include.description: Optional exact, case-insensitive tracker assignee allowlist. When set, only cards currently assigned to one of these people are eligible; all others remain visible as Excluded evidence.

x-workbook.label: Only count work assigned to
x-workbook.hint: Exact tracker display names, one per line. Blank = all assignees.

x-workbook.label: A change request is recognised by
x-workbook.hint: Regex, label or field value. Blank = CRs come from the estimates source instead.

x-workbook.label: People on the client side
x-workbook.hint: Exact names as they appear in the tracker. Used to tell a client-found defect from a QA-found one.

tags.description: The words your team tags titles with, in square or round brackets. Matching is tolerant: a tag one or two letters off a word here ('[Exisiting]') is read as that word, and the row says so in its Check column so a person can disagree. Defaults cover the usual English words; list your own if they differ.

pre_existing.description: Tags that mean a defect was already in the product before this work, e.g. Existing, Pre-existing, Legacy.

cr.description: Tags that mean an approved addition, e.g. CR, Change Request.

rejected.description: Tags or column names that mean a report was rejected, e.g. Invalid, By Design, Duplicate.

deferred.description: Column names that mean a report was moved out of scope, e.g. Deferred, Out of Scope.

workflow.description: What your team's states mean. This is the single most important section: it is what turns 'our board has a column called In Test' into a number management can compare across projects.

delivered_when.description: Your delivery event: when an item counts as delivered. Velocity counts items that reached it, and it is the default meaning of 'delivered on time' for a commitment. Most teams set this to the state that means development is finished and testing can start, but it is your choice - name the state, not a convention borrowed from somebody else's board.

values.description: e.g. ['Ready for QA', 'In Test', 'Dev Complete']. First entry into any of these.

from_date.description: Apply this rule only from a date onward, when the team changed its process mid-project. Before it, the fallback below applies.

x-workbook.label: Delivered when the item reaches
x-workbook.hint: List your column or status names. This is your delivery event, whatever it is.

completed_flag_means.description: What the tracker's own 'complete' flag means on your board - on some boards it means merged, not accepted.

reopened_when.description: Rework Rate compares reopening events after the agreed closure boundary with completed tasks whose outcome is known. Repeated reopening uses reopen_count where available; an explicit Yes without a count contributes one. First-round QA failure before closure is not rework.

values.description: States that mean 'back in play after being closed'.

no_history.description: A completed task with no record either way. 'unknown' leaves it out of the rate; 'not-reopened' counts it as not reopened, and the note says so.

x-workbook.label: Reopened when the item moves out of closed into

clarification_when.description: Task Comprehension = the requirement was understood without going back to the client. This is how we detect 'we had to ask'.

also_comments.description: Also treat a comment asking the client to clarify expected behaviour as 'had to ask'.

exclude_reasons.description: Going to Awaiting Feedback for a build or environment dependency is not a comprehension problem.

x-workbook.label: Had to ask the client when the item reaches

commitment.description: What a team commitment is, and what counts as meeting one. Delivery Commitment measures the reliability of the team: of the things the team negotiated and promised, how many landed on time. Both halves of that need saying, because teams commit to different things and not every task carries a commitment.

scope.description: committed-only = count just the items the team negotiated a date for, which is what PMS asks for. all-deliverables = treat every item as committed, for a team that commits to the whole scope as one. Items left out are named in the note either way.

met_when.description: What delivering a commitment means for this team, written as a short phrase that goes into the note. 'delivery' uses your delivery event above; 'handover' means the period's build reached the client; 'completion' means the item was closed. Anything else is used as written, so 'the demo environment was updated' is fine if that is what was promised.

x-workbook.label: Team commitments
x-workbook.hint: What the team promises, and what counts as keeping the promise.

sources.description: Where scope, hours and dates come from, and which of them the run is allowed to believe. All optional - a team with none of these still gets KPIs, with the gaps stated plainly.

x-workbook.title: Where the plan and the numbers come from

mode.description: Which sources may answer a question. tracker-only: the issue tracker is the single source of truth and nothing else is opened, so a run is fast, cheap and reproducible; anything the tracker cannot answer comes back 'Not measured' with the reason. tracker-first: the tracker answers, and the other sources are consulted only for facts it left blank. multi-source: other sources are read even when the tracker has an answer, and a disagreement is reported.

x-workbook.label: Source of truth
x-workbook.hint: tracker-only | tracker-first | multi-source. tracker-only never opens chat, mail or documents.

ref.description: A Drive link or id, a web link, or a path relative to the profile. Fetched straight to disk, and only when it has changed since the copy already there.

map.description: How to read the plan when it is a table, written once at setup so nobody re-reads the document on every run. For plan and estimates: {tab, columns: {title, board_key, dev_hours, qa_hours, period, approved_on, milestone}} where each value is the column's header text in the sheet. A source with no mapping (a PDF) is digested once by the assistant into facts/*.yaml instead.

ref.description: A Drive link or id, a web link, or a path relative to the profile. Fetched straight to disk, and only when it has changed since the copy already there.

map.description: How to read the estimates sheet when it is a table, written once at setup so nobody re-reads the document on every run. For plan and estimates: {tab, columns: {title, board_key, dev_hours, qa_hours, period, approved_on, milestone}} where each value is the column's header text in the sheet. A source with no mapping (a PDF) is digested once by the assistant into facts/*.yaml instead.

ref.description: A Drive link or id, a web link, or a path relative to the profile. Fetched straight to disk, and only when it has changed since the copy already there.

map.description: How to read the timeline or project tracker when it is a table, written once at setup so nobody re-reads the document on every run. For a timeline: {events: {tab, columns: {event, period, type, baseline, actual, state}, handover_types: [...]}, log: {tab, columns: {date, type, period, what, why, kpi}}}. The latest done handover event of a period becomes its handover date; log rows ticked for KPI become context for the notes. A source with no mapping (a PDF) is digested once by the assistant into facts/*.yaml instead.

evidence_channels.description: tool ids of chat spaces or mail labels a DEEP run may consult. A normal run never searches them: what the declared sources cannot answer becomes a question on the Open Questions tab. `kpi.py run --deep` may look those questions up here, and only here.

x-workbook.label: Where to look for evidence
x-workbook.hint: Tool ids from the Tools tab, one per line.

x-workbook.label: When the plan and the tracker disagree on hours, trust
x-workbook.hint: plan | tracker

x-workbook.label: Velocity counts
x-workbook.hint: dev = development hours only. dev+qa = adds each item's QA hours once its QA is done.

scan.description: How far a run is allowed to reach. Without limits every refresh re-reads every board, every channel and every thread from the beginning, which is slow, expensive and no more accurate. Every limit has a working default, and whatever a limit cut off is named in the run's Gaps rather than dropped quietly.

window.description: The time range a run reads. 'period' is the period's own start and end. 'period+grace' adds grace_days either side, which is what catches a handover announced the morning after the period closed. 'days' uses the 'days' field. 'all' removes the limit.

x-workbook.label: Time range to read
x-workbook.hint: period | period+grace | days | all

x-workbook.label: Days either side of the period
x-workbook.hint: Used when the range is period+grace.

x-workbook.label: Days back
x-workbook.hint: Used when the range is 'days'.

tracker_scope.description: How much of the board to read. 'all' is right for most boards and is the default, because a board is usually small and its history is what proves a date. 'touched-since' reads only items modified inside the window, which is what makes a big long-running board affordable. 'period' reads only items assigned to the period.

x-workbook.label: How much of the board to read
x-workbook.hint: all | touched-since | period

comments.description: Ticket comments are the most expensive thing on a board and are usually needed for a handful of items. 'on-demand' reads them only for items whose judgement actually depends on one, such as a clarification or a disputed date.

x-workbook.label: Read ticket comments
x-workbook.hint: always | on-demand | never

chat.description: Limits on chat spaces. Ignored entirely when the source of truth is tracker-only.

only_when_missing.description: Search a chat space only for a fact no other source could answer.

x-workbook.label: Chat: only for facts still missing

mail.description: Limits on mailboxes and threads. Ignored when the source of truth is tracker-only.

stop_when_found.description: Stop looking for a fact once a source has answered it, instead of collecting every mention.

x-workbook.label: Most sources to consult for one fact
x-workbook.hint: Raise it only where two sources routinely disagree and you want both quoted.

periods.description: How this team slices a project for PMS.

naming.default: Initial Scope, Additional Requests N, Milestone N, Full Project

x-workbook.label: Period naming
x-workbook.hint: PMS allows 25 characters.

x-workbook.label: Client date is met on
x-workbook.hint: Handover = when the build reached the client. Delivery = when the item itself was delivered.

by_section.description: Optional. Board columns that decide the period on their own: [{section: '^Sprint 14', period: 'Sprint 14'}]. 'section' is a regular expression on the column name.

velocity_unit.description: Default estimation unit; a project can override it.

policy.description: Counting choices the company allows a team to make. Everything not listed here is fixed by the engine and cannot be varied - that is deliberate.

x-workbook.label: Count defects that already existed in the product
Count defects found after handover in Defect Rate
Count rejected reports
x-workbook.hint: Fixed at No. Rejected reports are not defects.

output.description: What the run produces and how far it is allowed to go on its own. This is the setting most likely to differ between two leads, and it is deliberately easy to change.

mode.description: review-only produces a review workbook; dry-run also previews PMS changes; assisted-push allows an explicitly approved write. Legacy auto-push still requires explicit per-run approval; a schedule only prepares drafts.

x-workbook.label: How results reach PMS
x-workbook.hint: review-only | dry-run | assisted-push | auto-push

x-workbook.label: Legacy scheduling flag
x-workbook.hint: Does not authorize PMS writes. Schedules prepare drafts only.

unattended.description: Legacy scheduling compatibility flag. It never grants permission to send values to PMS.

workbook.description: Where the KPI tracker lives. xlsx (the default) writes it locally, in the project's folder. google-sheets also keeps one live Google Sheet that every run updates in place - same link every time. The local copy is always written, whichever is chosen.

x-workbook.label: Where the working file goes
x-workbook.hint: Google Drive folder link or ID. Local output follows the private profile/project folder.

workbook_location.description: A Drive folder (link or id). The first run creates the Google Sheet there; later runs find it by name and update it.

x-workbook.label: Tracker template to copy
x-workbook.hint: Not applied by the current kpi.py workbook writer.

workbook_template.description: Legacy configuration metadata; kpi.py uses its shared sheet model and does not copy an arbitrary template.

run_folder.description: Legacy runner setting. The current kpi.py writes under <profile folder>/<project id>/runs/<date>.

x-workbook.label: Post a summary to
x-workbook.hint: A tool id from the Tools tab, or blank for none.

notify.description: Preferred notification tool ID. The Python runner does not send messages; an assistant integration needs explicit user authorization.

workbook_file.description: A specific Google Sheet (link or id) to update in place, instead of creating one in workbook_location. Tabs the tool owns are rebuilt; tabs a person added are left alone.

workbook_name.description: Name for a Google Sheet the tool creates. {project} is replaced. Default: '[KPI Tracker] {project}'.

archive.description: Folder beside the live Google Sheet where a dated copy is kept before the sheet is updated, at most one a day (e.g. 'Archived'). Empty keeps no copies; Google's version history still applies.

custom_instructions.description: Instructions for the assistant: note style, glossary and review preferences. Supported rule overrides require a reason and remain visible. Official targets are managed in PMS and refreshed into the registry; separate local review targets belong in targets, require a reason, and block PMS submission until reconciled. KPI identities and shared formulas are not free-text settings.

notes_style.description: How you want the 'why' text to read. Free text. Example: 'Keep it under two sentences. Name the ticket, not the person. British spelling.'

x-workbook.label: House style for notes
x-workbook.hint: Free text. Applied when notes are written or rewritten.

always.description: Things to do on every run. Example: 'Always show the previous period next to the new one.' 'Always flag a KPI that moved more than 20 points.'

x-workbook.label: Always do this
x-workbook.hint: One instruction per line.

never.description: Things never to do. Example: 'Never post to the team chat.' 'Never push on a Friday.'

x-workbook.label: Never do this
x-workbook.hint: One instruction per line.

glossary.description: Words your team uses that an outsider would misread. Example: 'Handover means the client build, not the internal release.' 'MK = PartnerSync integration.'

x-workbook.label: What our words mean
x-workbook.hint: One per line. Stops a note being technically right and still misleading.

rule_overrides.description: Project facts the defaults get wrong. Each is applied and then printed in the run summary, so nobody has to guess why a number differs from the standard reading.

rule.description: Which behaviour to change. Supported: delivered_signal, client_date_source, commit_date_source, cr_denominator, exclude_key, include_key, defect_phase, hours_source, period_of_key, velocity_team_hours.

value.description: The new value, or 'KEY = value' when the rule is about one ticket.

why.description: Required. It appears in the run summary, so write it for somebody who was not in the room.

approved_by.description: Who agreed to it. Leave blank for a decision that is yours alone to make.

expires.description: Optional date after which the run warns that this override may be stale.

escalation.description: What to do when something needs a decision you cannot make. Example: 'Ask me in chat; if I do not answer in a day, hold the run and do not push.'

x-workbook.label: When a decision is needed
x-workbook.hint: Free text.

accounts.description: Your client accounts. Most of what varies between two projects actually varies between two clients - Northwind on Asana and Google Chat, Acme on Jira and Slack - so say it once here and every project on that account inherits it. A lead with one account can leave this out entirely.

id.description: Short handle, e.g. 'northwind'. Projects point at it.

notes.description: Anything a newcomer to this account should know.

conventions.description: Different ticket, defect or exclusion conventions.

workflow.description: Different state names. The most common override after tracker.

sources.description: A different plan, estimates sheet or evidence channels.

periods.description: A different period model or velocity unit.

policy.description: Different counting choices, where the company allows them.

output.description: A different output mode or working-file location.

custom_instructions.description: House style or rule overrides for this scope only.

targets.description: Local review targets for this scope, with value and why for each KPI.

overrides.description: What is true for every project on this account, but not for your others. Set the tracker, the chat spaces and the conventions here rather than repeating them on each project.

projects.description: Projects this profile covers, including review-only projects without PMS access. Shared defaults apply unless account or project overrides differ.

id.description: Short handle, e.g. 'q3-release'. Names the config and run files.

tracker_ref.description: The board this project lives on: the long number in an Asana board's URL, a Jira project key, or owner/repository on GitHub (several, comma-separated, are fine).

workbook_ref.description: Sheet id or file path of this project's tracker workbook.

conventions.description: Different ticket, defect or exclusion conventions.

workflow.description: Different state names. The most common override after tracker.

sources.description: A different plan, estimates sheet or evidence channels.

periods.description: A different period model or velocity unit.

policy.description: Different counting choices, where the company allows them.

output.description: A different output mode or working-file location.

custom_instructions.description: House style or rule overrides for this scope only.

targets.description: Local review targets for this scope, with value and why for each KPI.

overrides.description: What differs for this one project, on top of its account. Usually empty - if you find yourself repeating the same override on several projects, it belongs on the account instead.

account.description: The account this project belongs to, by id. It inherits that account's overrides.

deliverable_grain.description: What one deliverable is. board-cards (default): one card, one deliverable. plan-items: a card the plan breaks into modules counts once per module, so denominators follow the plan's own breakdown. It is printed on the Config tab, because it changes every ratio.

learned.description: Settings captured from conversation, each with the sentence it came from. Written by scripts/remember.py, never by hand. It answers 'why is this set like this' six months later, which is the question a configuration file normally cannot answer.

scope.description: profile defaults, or the account or project it applies to.

targets.description: Optional local review targets. Each needs a value and reason; source is printed beside the result. Remove these and refresh PMS targets before sending.
